entry.title: Before You Rebrand: How a Brand Audit Reveals What Actually Needs to Change
entry.summary: Dribbble Community Leader and The Branded Agency Head of Brand and Growth Quincy Samycia explains how to distinguish positioning, messaging, execution and identity issues before commissioning a rebrand.
entry.content:
Dribbble Community Leader and The Branded Agency Head of Brand and Growth Quincy Samycia explains how to distinguish positioning, messaging, execution and identity issues before commissioning a rebrand.

About the Author:
Quincy Samycia is Head of Brand and Growth at The Branded Agency, a branding, creative, website and growth agency working with ambitious companies across Canada, the United States and international markets. He helps organizations connect brand strategy with the creative, digital experiences and marketing systems responsible for measurable growth.

Before rebranding, conduct a brand audit to determine whether the problem is positioning, messaging, inconsistent execution, customer experience, or identity. A full rebrand becomes more defensible when the existing brand prevents the business from expressing a credible strategic direction.

A dated website, an unclear sales story, or a weaker campaign response can trigger a rebrand conversation. These observations describe discomfort, not its cause.

Moving directly to design risks replacing familiar assets without resolving the underlying problem. First establish what is broken, what still has value, and what customers already recognize.

“We need a rebrand” usually describes a symptom

A founder may mean the company has outgrown its market. Sales may mean prospects misunderstand the offer. Marketing may mean channels use conflicting assets. Customers may mean the experience doesn’t justify the price.

Each needs a different response. New visuals can’t differentiate an undifferentiated offer, fix a confusing checkout, or create ownership of brand guidelines. So the first job is working out which change the business can justify.

A brand audit separates symptoms from causes

A brand audit is a structured review of the gap between the brand a company intends to create and the brand people actually encounter. It compares strategy, language, identity, experience, and perception to produce evidence for decisions, including what to preserve and what to improve. It has five layers:

1. Internal intent. Agree on the priority audience, business direction, and credible advantages. If leaders disagree, the identity is being asked to express a strategy that hasn’t been resolved.

2. Public expression. Review the website, social profiles, ads, sales materials, recruitment communications, and support experience. Look at what’s in circulation today, not just the launch guidelines.

3. Market perception. Compare internal assumptions with customer interviews, reviews, sales conversations, employee feedback, and support questions. Find the gaps between the meaning you intended and what people actually understand.

4. Competitive context. Compare promises, visual conventions, and category language. Consistency gives little advantage if your story is interchangeable with your competitors’.

5. Experience and evidence. Check whether the experience proves the promise. Simplicity requires an easy buying journey, expertise needs evidence, and premium positioning needs credible service and delivery.

Four different problems are commonly mistaken for one rebrand problem

Classify the findings before setting the creative scope.

1. A positioning problem. The company can’t explain who it serves, what value it offers, or why customers should choose it. Generic homepage claims and inconsistent sales explanations are common symptoms. Research the audience and market, identify credible differentiation, and make strategic choices before redesigning.

2. A messaging problem. The strategy is sound, but internal terminology obscures the value or proof arrives too late. Rebuild the value proposition, message hierarchy, voice, and audience-specific language.

3. An execution and governance problem. A useful identity has fragmented: outdated logos circulate, campaigns invent their own styles, and sales materials contradict the website. Consolidate assets, improve templates, clarify approval rules, and assign ownership. Better governance may be the answer, not a new identity.

4. A genuine identity problem. The name or identity creates the wrong category expectation, undermines credibility, or can’t support the business’s direction. A merger, a new market, or a changed business model can expose these limits. The test is strategic usefulness, not whether the identity feels old.

The evidence should determine the scope

A rebranding strategy should connect each finding to the right response: reposition, rewrite, systematize, redesign, or a combination. The audit diagnoses the problem. A rebrand changes the strategy or identity when that diagnosis supports it.

If the experience contradicts the promise, fix the experience. Communication can’t hide that gap indefinitely.

Protect existing brand equity: recognition, search demand, familiar language, and trusted associations. Record what deserves to stay alongside what needs to change, then choose the project that closes the most important gap with the least unnecessary disruption.

AI search has turned brand consistency into a visibility issue

Search engines and AI assistants encounter websites, profiles, reviews, listings, and third-party references. They infer the company’s identity from those public sources.

Coherent names, categories, audiences, expertise, and proof make that identity easier to interpret. Conflicting descriptions can produce ambiguity. An “enterprise consultancy” on the homepage, a “creative studio” on LinkedIn, and a “software provider” in directories present three different expectations.

Audit facts and positioning across sources while letting language adapt to context. Support important claims with credible evidence. Consistency can improve interpretability, though it doesn’t guarantee rankings or AI citations.

Can a brand audit improve SEO, AEO, and GEO?

It can identify contradictory company information, unclear expertise, and missing proof. Addressing those gaps supports machine understanding without guaranteeing visibility.

Mini case study: humanizing data inside PepsiCo

Our work with PepsiCo’s Data Science & Advanced Analytics team could have been framed as visual modernization. The diagnosis showed a perception problem. The team powered insights across major brands, yet data science could feel technical and intimidating to internal stakeholders, and potential recruits could miss its role in shaping global commerce.

We repositioned the story around what data enabled: clearer foresight, better decisions, and greater confidence. The identity balanced precision with warmth across messaging, presentations, internal communications, recruitment materials, and the team’s app. The gaps in strategy and communication defined the visual system’s job. Without diagnosis, the team might have received a polished version of the same inaccessible story.

View the PepsiCo Labs Data Science and Advanced Analytics case study

When a full rebrand is actually justified

There’s no universal threshold, but the case gets stronger when:

  • The business or category has changed substantially
  • A merger requires new brand architecture
  • The name limits growth
  • Priority audiences no longer recognize themselves
  • Research shows the identity reduces trust
  • The visual system lacks the range needed across products, markets, and digital experiences

One issue may justify an update. Several connected constraints can support broader change.

Identify what must survive, whether a name, color, symbol, phrase, or product story. Continuity protects useful memory, and a clearer system can feel new without erasing every recognizable asset.

How do you know whether your company needs a rebrand?

Look for evidence that the identity or name blocks the business’s direction. Messaging or governance problems may need narrower changes.

Run the audit before writing the creative brief

Use the audit to define the audience, business change, perception gap, assets to retain, required evidence, and the observable job of the new system.

Start with current touchpoints and competitor materials. Compare claims, language, identity, and proof, and ask customers and employees how they describe the company. Note confusion, friction, and overlooked strengths.

Teams that want an outside-in starting point can review public brand, website, search, reputation, and AI-visibility signals and turn them into a prioritized diagnostic, as in The Branded Agency’s Brand Health Audit. This doesn’t replace customer interviews or a full strategic engagement, but it can show where deeper investigation is most likely to matter.

Translate findings into decisions with priorities and owners, rather than delivering observations alone. Brand designers can then carry those decisions into the identity and system.

How often should you conduct a brand audit?

Consider an annual review, plus additional checks before expansion, mergers, website redesigns, or major audience changes.

A good audit should make the answer smaller and clearer

The answer may be a new identity, clearer positioning, stronger proof, or templates people can use. A company shouldn’t replace its whole brand to solve every brand problem.

We audit first, preserve useful recognition, and change only what keeps the company from being easier to understand, trust, and choose.

entry.title: Why Website Redesigns Fail Before the First Screen Is Designed
entry.summary: Dribbble Community Leader and The Branded Agency Head of Brand and Growth Quincy Samycia explains why strong redesigns begin with positioning, decision architecture, proof and measurement before the first screen is designed.
entry.content:
Dribbble Community Leader and The Branded Agency Head of Brand and Growth Quincy Samycia explains why strong redesigns begin with positioning, decision architecture, proof and measurement before the first screen is designed.

About the Author:
Quincy Samycia is Head of Brand and Growth at The Branded Agency, a branding, creative, website and growth agency working with ambitious companies across Canada, the United States and international markets. He helps organizations connect brand strategy with the creative, digital experiences and marketing systems responsible for measurable growth.

Website redesigns fail when teams change the interface before they settle on audience priorities, positioning, content, customer journeys and measures of success. A strong website redesign strategy defines those foundations first, then uses UX/UI design, development and testing to turn them into a clearer, more useful experience.

A dated interface, crowded navigation and slow publishing are symptoms. At The Branded Agency, our website strategy, UX/UI design and development work starts with a different question: what decision should this website help the right person make?

That question shifts the conversation from preference to purpose. It makes us define the audience, the value of the offer, the evidence needed to believe it and the path from interest to action. It also shows that many apparent design problems are unresolved business, brand or content problems.

A website redesign brief usually describes symptoms

“Make it modern” may signal outdated positioning. “Simplify it” may point to an undefined priority audience. “Improve conversion” may mean the offer lacks proof. “Make it easier to update” may mean no one owns the content.

Moving to Webflow or Shopify doesn’t answer any of those questions. Platform requirements should come out of the diagnosis, not stand in for it. When we skip that step, design inherits decisions the business has avoided, and the result is a polished website that is still hard to understand.

Brand, decision and operations: the three jobs of a website

We treat a website as three connected systems:

  • Brand: makes the company recognizable and communicates a distinct point of view.
  • Decision: helps visitors judge relevance, credibility and the next step.
  • Operations: lets marketing publish, sales share useful destinations and internal teams keep content accurate.

When one system dominates, the trade-offs are predictable: memorable but vague storytelling, interchangeable conversion tactics, or efficient but uninspiring templates. Our goal is a website strategy that links expression, action and operation in one customer experience.

Six questions every website redesign should answer

Before we sketch a wireframe, we want clear answers to these questions:

  • Who is the priority audience?
  • What are they trying to accomplish?
  • What makes this offer meaningfully different?
  • What must they understand before they can act?
  • What proof will reduce their doubt?
  • Which action represents real business value?

Vague answers produce generic hero copy, navigation organized by department and competing calls to action. That is why we let positioning and messaging shape the sitemap: they decide what matters, in what order and to whom.

The website redesign process

When copywriters fill predetermined boxes and analytics arrives near launch, teams lose the chance to shape the experience. We start the website redesign process by mapping the visitor’s decision.

  1. Start from where the visitor is
    Visitors may be researching a category, comparing options, validating a recommendation or getting ready to buy, and each stage needs a different path. Someone arriving from a specific campaign may need product evidence right away, while someone researching the category may need context first. The content sequence should account for those entry points.
  2. Name the decision they are trying to make
    Vague goals such as ‘learn more’ become a concrete question: does this product fit my workflow? Can I justify its price? The page is then built around the answer.
  3. Sequence claim, meaning and proof
    “Faster” invites “compared with what?” “Trusted” invites “by whom?” We explain what each benefit means and place supporting evidence next to the claim.
  4. Remove friction and keep the character
    Clarity depends on hierarchy. Cutting words or colours alone rarely achieves it. We keep the next step visible and preserve a distinctive voice and visual identity. Then we test whether someone can identify the offer, find relevant evidence and locate the next step without help from the project team. If they can’t, revisit sequence and emphasis before adding content or stripping back the identity.
  5. Define success before choosing the solution
    We define the intended outcome before selecting platforms, components and analytics. What success looks like depends on the business: an enterprise site may prioritize publishing workflows, an eCommerce site may need strong product discovery, and a lead generation site may need qualification and sales follow-up. We choose Webflow, Shopify or another platform against those requirements, not the other way around.

Proof should be part of the design system

Proof belongs where visitors encounter doubt, not on a disconnected testimonial page. We match the evidence to the claim:

  • Performance: benchmarks, results or demonstrations.
  • Expertise: relevant case studies, credentials or process.
  • Trust: reviews, recognizable clients and transparent policies.
  • Usability: an experience that is easy to complete.
  • Brand: consistency between the promise and the experience.

We map proof during wireframing because evidence changes layouts and content requirements. Sometimes an unsupported claim has to change as well.

Build a content system, not a collection of pages

A refined homepage must eventually support dozens of less prominent pages, and reusable components alone won’t make that system scale.

A content system defines page purposes, field relationships, content limits, reusable proof patterns and rules for variation. Ownership is assigned so teams know who creates, approves and maintains content, and each element is marked as mandatory or optional, with a clear link between proof and products or services. A content model should reflect how the organization actually creates and updates information.

Whether you hire Webflow designers or Shopify designers, make sure templates are tested with real content and with the people who will publish it.

Flexibility should support informed choices without breaking hierarchy. The best handoff isn’t a library of blocks; it’s a set of choices the internal team can make with confidence.

What this looked like for Milton Coffee Co.

Milton Coffee Co. came to us with a specific eCommerce website redesign problem: the site did not communicate the value of its premium, customizable coffee machines clearly enough.

We began with discovery and creative exploration, kept the existing branding and photography, and refined the homepage and section copy. A customized Shopify template, dynamic product templates and a third-party “design your own” integration supported the buying journey.

Behind the screen, the templates also simplified future product uploads. The work connected what customers needed to understand with what the internal team needed to maintain, which took the project beyond a visual refresh.

Performance and accessibility are design requirements

We treat speed, stability, responsiveness and accessibility as design inputs from the start of the project.

Google’s Core Web Vitals guidance focuses on loading performance, interactivity and visual stability, because these are measurable parts of the experience real users receive. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines are organized around content being perceivable, operable, understandable and robust.

In practice, that means budgeting for media and animation, protecting contrast, using meaningful headings and supporting keyboard interaction. These decisions affect both comprehension and usability. A website that promises simplicity but loads slowly or excludes visitors contradicts its own message.

Treat launch as the start of learning

Launch begins observation of the complete website; it doesn’t end the redesign. Prototype testing reduces risk, but real behaviour will still raise questions the project team didn’t anticipate. The Nielsen Norman Group’s iterative homepage redesign case study is a useful illustration of design improving through rounds of prototyping, testing and refinement rather than a single reveal.

We set baseline measures before launch, then review:

  • Can priority visitors find the information they need?
  • Which messages and proof encourage useful action?
  • Where do qualified visitors hesitate or leave?
  • Can the team publish without weakening the system?

The answers set improvement priorities. Qualified inquiries, completed purchases and publishing efficiency deserve a look alongside conversion rate, since not every click carries equal weight.

Settle the foundations before you approve a mockup

Before approving a mockup, confirm the audience, positioning, offer, proof, content model and success measures, and include performance, accessibility and measurement in the brief.

A successful website redesign makes the business easier to understand, the next decision easier to make and the system easier to improve. Those outcomes begin with choices made before the first screen.

entry.title: 7 Ways To Close The Gap Between AI-Generated Apps and Great Product Design
entry.summary: Dribbble Community Leader and Expo Product & Brand Designer Nicolas Solerieu talks about closing the gap between AI-generated apps and great product design, from replacing default icons to designing for error states and edge cases AI tends to skip.
entry.content:
Dribbble Community Leader and Expo Product & Brand Designer Nicolas Solerieu talks about closing the gap between AI-generated apps and great product design, from replacing default icons to designing for error states and edge cases AI tends to skip.

About the Author:
Nicolas Solerieu is a product and brand designer at Expo, working across product, web, and brand identity. Previously at GitHub and Opendoor, he’s interested in software, the web, and the strange craft of arranging rectangles for a living.

You can’t one-shot an app. The capabilities are on the table, and mature frameworks and skilled LLMs are within reach. Chances are you’ve used vibe-coded software, and noticed differences. The obvious flaws are disappearing. What remains is subtler: the gap between an AI-generated app that works and one that feels considered.

1. Build a Brand System for Your AI-Generated App

Good product design blurs the edges between brand and product. Ask an LLM, even in plan mode, and it will improvise a branding kit to suit its own needs. Even in tools like Claude Design, where you can provide a base kit, it will still create brand artifacts of its own. Illustration should be consistent, and colors and layout should create a visual continuity from marketing to product, guiding users along the way.

The various touchpoints require different fidelity. Marketing is usually higher fidelity while products tend to be more minimal and rely on color and icons alone. Infusing a product with personality and a distinct style is almost an art. It requires care, attention, and taste: human qualities that can only be amplified, not outsourced.

A brand is also a living entity that flexes beyond the system an AI can understand: employee swag, micro events, an internal sports team, fan art. These are where a product’s personality shows up in ways no brand kit specifies. Think of a brand as the set of artifacts that breathes life into your product. A simple motto is a good way to keep this in mind: “small screens, big moments.”

2. Replace Default Icons and Generic AI Illustrations

Most LLMs pull icons out of their preferred library, or invent them with SVG and CSS. Without specific direction, the result is often generic. 90% of the apps I saw use Lucide icons. It’s solid and covers most cases, but at this scale, it’s becoming the obvious default. You can do better and easily. The same goes for illustration. Certain styles and obvious quality flaws can erode trust quickly.

3. Use Purposeful, Restrained Animation in Your App UI

LLMs greatly ease the production of animation. They tend to go hard on the same attributes since CSS and SVG make them most accessible, and shaders are also more prominent nowadays. The downside is that interfaces can accumulate motion before anyone has asked for it. It happens to me all the time with all my frontend design skills loaded up by default. Animation is rarely improved by quantity. More often than not, restraint and purpose are needed on the human side to improve the quality of outcomes.

4. Test on Real Devices to Make Your Mobile App Feel Native

You may have noticed a strong enthusiasm for products that “feel native.” This feeling often boils down to performance and familiarity. Design is the experience, and ease and speed are a big part of it. Only a human can truly feel that quality, so test, test and test again. Your firsthand experience with each ecosystem matters.

Simulators help here, too. When an agent can launch your app in a simulator, tap through flows, and test what it built, a typically painful part of the process becomes visual and collaborative. You can watch it work, spot what feels off, and steer it in real time. It speeds up the loop, but it doesn’t replace the device in your hand, so keep testing on real hardware before you call it done.

5. Enforce Design System Consistency and Visual Hierarchy

All of the above is well and good, but what often betrays a UX is inconsistency across the whole UI. LLMs are getting better at sticking to a design system, but as anyone who has worked in this industry knows, having a design system guarantees nothing. The wrong component or primitive still ends up in the wrong place. Systems are flexible, and LLMs will be only as flawed as humans.

That’s why the visual basics still need a human eye. LLMs are getting better at checking them, but human taste remains the best judge. Great visual design guides the eye so information feels effortless to digest. Contrast and visual hierarchy make the most important details pop first. Alignment and proximity keep related pieces grouped so the layout feels orderly rather than chaotic. Whitespace gives elements room to breathe, creating a balanced design that feels clean, clear, and intentional.

6. Plan Migrations and Involve Users and Partners Before You Prompt

Design sits at the intersection of operations, engineering, marketing, and infrastructure. Great design is often the direct product of a purposeful blend of those priorities, and that’s hard to convey to LLMs, which either wait for precise instruction or take (sometimes wild) guesses. 

Some scenarios, like migrations, are more straightforward. Others require more planning and handholding. Porting over your web app to mobile? Going native? These can seem like perfect tasks for AI but often result in many edge cases. Careful review via simulators and platform knowledge goes a long way. It’s never just a design matter. I’d encourage you to think about the contingencies and holistic drivers.

The same goes for the people involved. You might have heard “don’t ship your org chart.” While a great app is a set of features, UX is the sum of all things, too many things to truly list in one blog post. Points of friction, and human shortcomings often materialize in the experience. Talking to your users, and your relationships with project partners and vendors, are an invisible yet obvious part of the design process that LLMs can’t fully replace. Sometimes they even introduce a new kind of friction.

7. Design for Error States, Empty States, and Accessibility, Not Just the Happy Path

The modern product designer is not someone who starts from a blank canvas but an “Editor-in-Chief” who curates, prunes, and directs AI outputs. More like a webmaster of the 2000s than a 2016 product designer. Steering and QC is more important than ever to avoid the “Happy Path” Trap: LLMs excel at ideal user flows, but product design happens in the margins. AI frequently ignores error states, zero-data screens, dynamic text wrapping, role-based views, focus & accessibility requirements, loading indicators, and all too often, container alignment. Brand remains the wild west, and it should. That’s where the beautiful complexity of design shows.

Polish is when persistence and taste meet the craft of design. AI elevates the floor so anyone can build software, and human craft is what raises the ceiling. Since tools are becoming generalists, perhaps designers need to become generalists (again) too.

entry.title: How We Help Clients Spend Their Budget on the Right Things
entry.summary: Dribbble Community Leader and Heyo Co-Founder Peter Deltondo reveals their radically transparent approach to project budgets, helping clients scope the right features, costs, and expectations.
entry.content:
Dribbble Community Leader and Heyo Co-Founder Peter Deltondo reveals their radically transparent approach to project budgets, helping clients scope the right features, costs, and expectations.

About the Author:
Peter Deltondo is a Product Designer turned Product Founder who spent the last decade leading teams, Co-Founding Heyo, a design and development agency, and Co-Founding products, including Eventrise and Keyvo. The list of clients he’s worked with includes Figma, Adobe, Discord, Facebook, Merck, and Toyota. In his free time, he can be found in a river fly fishing or spending time with his family in the great outdoors.

Most projects that go wrong went wrong in the first budget conversation, and usually because everyone in the room was too optimistic. The budget was too low to get things done right, but the client hoped it would stretch, and a well-meaning product designer or agency hoped they could figure out a way to make it work. In the end, they couldn’t.

I believe the budget conversation is the first piece of design work on any project. Get it right and the project is set up for success. Get it wrong and no amount of talent or optimism can fix things.

I tell clients our rates before I ask for their budget

If I ask a client for their budget and then float a number back, how do they know I didn’t just anchor to whatever they said? They don’t. And that suspicion, even when it is wrong, poisons the relationship before a single screen gets designed. Every future conversation about scope now has a little voice in it asking whether the agency is optimizing for the client and the project, or for the paycheck.

So after I learn about their project needs, I go first. Here is what we would charge to accomplish this project, here is the scope that covers, here is how many designers and/or developers it takes and how long is needed to get this work done. Most importantly, it’s a realistic number that we fully believe is achievable, not a pipe dream best case scenario. Cautiously realistic. The number we would actually bet on.

I’ve had many clients tell me that was the moment they decided to move forward. Not the portfolio, not the case studies. The moment they realized we were not playing games with them.

People talk about pricing as a sales problem. It’s a trust problem, and trust is what actually closes.

I’m not a fan of value-based pricing

I know that’s a hot take in agency circles, but here’s how we think about it. We value our work at a weekly rate. It’s a premium rate for premium quality work. The only question is how many weeks it takes to successfully complete the work at our desired level of excellence. We can explain our reasoning for our time and budget, and it has nothing to do with how big the client is or how important the project or outcome is to them. There’s a tried and true formula to it, not a made up “I think I can get the client to shell out this much.”

A client can check our math. It checks out.

What that trust is actually worth

I’ll never forget when a longtime client of ours came to us with a project that should have been started weeks prior. If it got started ASAP, it still had a chance. Their back was against the wall, and it was a good sized project with lots of work to do. We made clear where our concerns and risks were with the scope based on the time available, and we were realistic with what could get done. We quoted around $400k. We won the project.

What they said next was the most important part, and I think one of the reasons why we still work with this client today: “Everyone else knew how desperate we were and tried to take advantage of us. The next lowest bid we got was $2M. In no world is this a $2M project. Everyone here knows that.”

Then they told us why they keep coming back, and it wasn’t just the work we do. It was that we were honest with them, that they could count on us to be a true partner, and that we never tried to take advantage of them. That’s the reputation that has their teams asking to work with us again and again. I can assure you, we’ve done way more work over the years with this client than anything we would have gained by value pricing them on that one project.

Most of our clients here at Heyo are long term or repeat customers. That trust has to be earned from the first sales call, and the budget conversation is where it starts.

The budget is the brief

The beauty of quoting the work and placing the budget alongside it is that any change in the client’s budget changes the scope of the project. We can’t magically get twice as much done at the same budget, but we can focus on a smaller scope of work with less time and budget. Sometimes it’s our job to help the client figure out how to get the most out of less. The line we won’t cross is cutting so far that less no longer gets them anywhere. If a client sees a return on the work, big budget or small, they come back. That’s the easiest way we’ve found to earn repeat clients over the years.

Some of the questions we might ask to help gain focus and clarity on the right scope for them include:

  • What has to be true on launch day for this to count as a win? Not the full vision, the launch day version.
  • If we could solve only one problem for your customers, which one would actually move the business forward?
  • Which of these features are here because a competitor has them, and which are here because a customer asked for them?
  • What could ship in a second phase without anyone noticing it was missing on day one?

The answers reorder the scope almost every time. A company came to us a while back wanting a full product redesign: new UI, new flows, the whole thing. Before we touched a screen we spent time on the actual problem, and the problem was that most users were dropping off in their first session, long before they ever reached the flows we were being asked to rebuild. The interface wasn’t the issue. Onboarding was. People weren’t sticking around long enough to see the screens the client wanted redesigned.

So we told them to pump the brakes on the redesign. Fix onboarding first. Observe, learn, adapt. Later on we continued in a second phase to revamp the product based on what we learned.

That is an uncomfortable thing to say to someone who walked in ready to pay for something bigger. But it cost them less, it mattered more, and it is the reason they came back to work with us again.

Quick and right are not opposites. Quick and cheap are.

There is real value in getting to market fast, and I don’t want to pretend otherwise. Every month a product isn’t live is a month of customer feedback you don’t have and revenue you didn’t collect. Speed matters, and any agency that treats “we need this soon” as a red flag has forgotten what it is like to run a business.

The problem is that “quick” almost always arrives bundled with “cheap,” and those are different asks. A small scope built properly can be quick. A full scope built halfway can’t, because the half you skipped is the half that breaks the first time real users show up. It is the auth flow nobody tested, the edge case nobody designed, the database that was fine at a hundred users and falls over at ten thousand.

The honest version of speed is a smaller, finished thing. Not a bigger, unfinished one. When a client tells us they need to be live in eight weeks, our first question isn’t whether we can do it. It is what the eight-week version of this product looks like, and whether that version is worth launching. Usually it is, and usually it is smaller than what they came in with.

Sometimes the answer is no

This is the part agencies don’t like to talk about.

If a budget can’t produce a result that changes anything for the client, taking the project anyway isn’t generosity. The client spends the money, gets something that doesn’t move the needle, and the main thing they learn is that hiring an agency was a bad bet. You didn’t help them. You just found a polite way to take their money.

So we say no to work we can’t move the needle on. That includes budgets that are too low for the outcome the client actually needs, and it includes projects where the client wants a thing built that we think is the wrong thing to build. Both are hard conversations. Both are cheaper than the alternative.

There are two exceptions we take seriously.

The first is a smaller first project. When the full thing is out of reach today, we will often propose a narrower engagement that proves the fit and solves one real problem. If it works, it earns the second project. If it doesn’t, everyone found out for a fraction of the cost.

The second is portfolio work. Sometimes a project is in a space we want to be in, or with a team we want to work with, and the budget is below where we would normally go. We will take that work. But we take it as a business decision, priced deliberately, with everyone on our side knowing why we said yes. What we won’t do is take it at a discount and quietly resent it, or take it and cut corners to make the number work. The client should know which kind of yes they are getting.

Redoing it is the most expensive version of the project

This is the pitfall from the top of the article, the too-low budget everyone hoped would work out. Here’s the math on it.

When a project has to be rebuilt, you pay for the work twice. That part is obvious. What is less obvious is everything else not on the invoice. You pay for the months between the first version and the second, when the product was live and not working. You pay in the users who tried the first version and are not coming back for the second, because people don’t give products many chances. You pay in your own team’s morale, because nobody wants to rebuild something they suspected was going to break the first time.

This is the whole reason we describe Heyo as the crew that builds your brand, product, and website right the first time. It isn’t a slogan about perfectionism. It is a statement about which version of the project is actually cheaper and leads clients to the best chance of success for their brand or product. The answer is almost never the one that skipped steps to hit a number.

The cheapest project is the one you only have to build once.

Realistic is a two-way street

Being realistic about budget isn’t only the agency’s job.

Our side of it is telling clients plainly what their number buys, even when the honest answer is smaller than what they walked in hoping to pay for. It is saying no when no is the right answer. It is putting the second phase in the conversation on day one so nobody tries to cram it into the first.

The client’s side is bringing an honest number, an honest deadline, and a willingness to hear what those two things can produce together. The clients we do our best work for aren’t the ones with the biggest budgets. They are the ones who told us the real number early and let us design around it.

Both halves of that are rarer than they should be. When they show up together, the project usually works.

The number does not change the work

Here is what I keep coming back to after all these years.

The budget was never the problem. Small and large budgets have produced work we are proud of and helped our clients succeed and grow. What decides it is whether both sides knew, before anything started, exactly what the number would buy and what it would not.

Say the number first. Treat it like a brief. Build the smaller thing properly instead of the bigger thing halfway. Say no when you can’t help. And put the second project on the table while you are still scoping the first.

That isn’t a pricing strategy. There is no “slick” sales or gift of gab. Just be real and honest. It is how you end up being the agency a client calls back.

entry.title: Website Redesign SEO: How to Protect Traffic and Build for AI Search
entry.summary: Dribbble Community Leader and Vix Media Group Founding Partner Anthony Dutcher explains how to protect search traffic during a website redesign, and how to structure content so both Google and AI assistants send people to the right page.
entry.content:
Dribbble Community Leader and Vix Media Group Founding Partner Anthony Dutcher explains how to protect search traffic during a website redesign, and how to structure content so both Google and AI assistants send people to the right page.

About the Author:
Anthony Dutcher is Founding Partner at Vix Media Group, a Denver-based agency working across healthcare, technology and media. His team is deliberately split between agency and in-house backgrounds and runs its own infrastructure, so it has sat on both sides of the brief. He believes research should decide the design, not decorate it.

A behavioral-health website we refreshed did not need a dramatic new look. It needed a better way for people to find the right care.

The visible changes were modest. The structural work was not: we added 80-plus content pages across services, locations, conditions, and outcomes evidence. We simplified the navigation and standardized calls to action.

More content. Less navigation friction. That is a more interesting design problem than choosing a new hero image.

At Vix Media Group, I want every redesign to protect what already brings people in and make the next step clearer. Today, that means thinking about Google, AI-assisted discovery, and the person who still has to decide whether to contact the business.

1. Give the redesign a business brief, not just a visual brief.

The behavioral-health project is a useful distinction between a visual refresh and a structural rebuild. They are not the same scope, and the screenshot does not tell the whole story.

Expanding the content library while simplifying navigation addresses two different needs:

  • Search visitors need a page that matches a specific question.
  • Website visitors need a clear route through the business, not an inventory of every page it publishes.

For a care provider, those questions can start with a condition, a treatment, or a location. Putting all three into one general page makes the visitor do the sorting. Putting every answer in the main menu creates a different problem.

The job is to give useful answers their own destinations, then organize those destinations into a site people can understand. Our SEO strategy and design decisions have to work from the same map.

Does adding more pages improve SEO?

Not by itself. A page earns its place when it answers a distinct need with useful information. A location name swapped into otherwise identical copy is not the same thing as meaningful coverage. The 80-plus pages describe the scope of this project, not a target for every business.

2. Simplify the interface without thinning the information.

A cleaner interface should make the content easier to use, not make the business harder to understand. In the healthcare refresh, simplified navigation sat above an expanded content library. Standardized calls to action provided a more consistent next step.

The live site makes that distinction concrete: visitors can explore services and conditions, check insurance information, and find provider credentials without treating the homepage as the entire website.

This is where good web designers earn their place. A heading identifies the subject. Spacing separates an answer from the next question. A repeated button treatment makes the next action recognizable. The page can be calm without being empty.

One change was more revealing than a new color palette: we corrected a provider’s professional title across key pages and added a credentialed bio to a service page. Accuracy is part of the experience. A beautiful layout cannot compensate for describing the professional incorrectly.

Where should FAQs go?

Put an answer beside the decision it supports. Coverage questions belong near insurance information. A question about the first appointment belongs near the inquiry step. Do not bury every useful answer in an accordion at the bottom just because the template has an FAQ section.

3. Preserve the route from search to the right page.

A redesign starts with an inventory of existing value. Before changing a URL, I want to know what searches reach it, what relevant links point to it, and what visitors do after landing there.

The same logic applies whether the project adds a substantial content library or mainly updates its presentation. Keep a useful address unless there is a good reason to change it. When it must move, map it to the closest relevant replacement, not automatically to the homepage.

My launch checks, which a web developer should be able to walk through with you, follow the visitor’s route:

  • Confirm that important pages load and can be indexed.
  • Test permanent redirects and update internal links to the final destinations.
  • Check canonical URLs, sitemap entries, and production indexing settings.
  • Submit a test inquiry and confirm that the team receives it.
  • Verify that analytics records the intended action, not just a pageview.

Can a relaunch avoid every traffic dip?

No agency can promise that. Google’s site-move guidance anticipates ranking fluctuations as changed URLs are recrawled and reindexed. A launch needs a baseline and ongoing monitoring, not a promise that the graph will never move.

4. Separate useful demand from impressive-looking traffic.

The number to protect is not always the largest number in the report. A popular news story and a service page that produces inquiries do different jobs.

I have seen this tension in our legal-sector work. A major redesign did not restore the site’s previous traffic level, and a history of high-volume news publishing complicated the picture. A new interface was not, by itself, a recovery strategy.

That experience changes the questions I ask before a refresh. Which page types lost visibility? Which visitors had a reason to hire the business? What changed in publishing, tracking, or search demand around the launch?

The healthcare project’s content expansion and standardized calls to action belong together for exactly this reason. Discovery needs a destination, and that destination needs a useful next step. More pages and more visits are not the finish line.

5. Make room for AI discovery without abandoning the fundamentals.

AI assistants are already a measurable entry point into websites we manage. Across a commercial building-products portfolio, we counted 757 sessions attributed to ChatGPT in GA4 reporting from August 30 through September 28, 2026. Of those, 449 were engaged sessions: visits that met GA4’s criteria for time spent, pages viewed, or a key event.

The behavioral-health site recorded 15 sessions from identifiable AI sources in the same 30-day window. That smaller number matters: the opportunity exists, but its scale varies by business.

These are referral observations, not proof that a redesign caused the visits or that every recorded action became a qualified lead. The practical response is to measure the channel and examine what visitors find when they arrive.

Does AI search require a separate kind of website?

My starting point is a site that explains the business exceptionally well. Clear services, accurate credentials, useful answers, connected pages, and accessible content help the reader regardless of the source of the visit.

For Google’s own AI features, Google says the existing SEO fundamentals still apply. That is not a universal recipe for every assistant. It is a useful correction to the idea that AI discovery requires abandoning the fundamentals that make a website useful.

6. Judge the relaunch by the journey it supports

After launch, put search visibility, landing-page traffic, and verified inquiries beside one another. Break them down by source and page purpose. That is why I see website development as more than getting pages live: the inquiry still has to reach the right team.

For the behavioral-health refresh, the story is not a dramatic aesthetic reinvention. It is an expanded content library, simpler navigation, clearer professional information, and a more consistent path to contact. Those decisions shape how the site works long after the homepage reveal.

A redesign should make the business easier to understand and easier to reach. The best proof is not how different the homepage looks.

Before your next relaunch, can you trace a real customer question from the search result to the right answer and a working next step?

entry.title: How To Stay Original While Designing With AI
entry.summary: Dribbble Community Leader and Unfold Founder & Creative Director Eddie Lobanovskiy shares how his team uses AI tools to speed up moodboarding and prototyping, and explains why taste and judgment still decide what's original.
entry.content:
Dribbble Community Leader and Unfold Founder & Creative Director Eddie Lobanovskiy shares how his team uses AI tools to speed up moodboarding and prototyping, and explains why taste and judgment still decide what's original.

About the Author:
Unfold Founder & Creative Director Eddie Lobanovskiy builds high-impact brand identities and UI/UX ecosystems at the intersection of classical design and AI innovation. Designer of the XRP logo.

Every designer using AI eventually asks the same question: if the tool can generate a hundred options in a minute, what is actually left that’s mine? 

I’ve spent my career building brand identities and UI/UX ecosystems, and I now work at the intersection of classical design and AI. 

As a branding agency optimizing processes with AI, our answer at Unfold is simple. AI helps us explore more possibilities, but our creative team still decides what is worth pursuing. 

Where AI tools fit in our design process

We use AI throughout the creative process: moodboarding, image generation, content, concept exploration, and dev prototypes. GPT, Grok, and Claude help with organization, content, support, and ideation, among other things.

The biggest benefit is speed. It lets us explore more directions earlier, without committing a lot of time to each one. 

Moodboarding, reimagined

Moodboarding has changed a lot for us. Instead of only searching for references that already exist, we can generate something closer to the exact visual idea we have in mind.

Branda (www.branda.co), our own brand tool, helps us generate ideas and sketches quickly. When we need tighter control over the visuals, we turn to Recraft, which gives us the most control over image generation.

We recently partnered with BPay, a peer-to-peer payment system. We had a general idea on the direction of the design, so we plugged it into AI, and it output a few directions that we can go in.

After we generated a handful of concepts, we pulled out what we thought could work really well and work well together, created a polished version of the direction, and sent it out to the client.

Basically, it avoided us hours of looking for moodboarding and other work, and we were able to pinpoint the exact direction we wanted.

The first output is never the final output

We rarely treat the first AI output as final. It’s usually a starting point that gets refined, redesigned, rewritten, combined, or rebuilt.
This is where the risk sits. If you accept the first result, everything starts to look the same. That’s why the designer’s role becomes even more important: you have to know when to push further.

Taste is the filter

AI gives us more possibilities, but taste is still the filter.

AI can generate endless options, but someone still has to know what is actually good, what feels generic, and what fits the brand. That judgment is the part no tool supplies. 

It’s also why we start with an idea or direction first, then use AI to help us explore it, rather than letting the tool decide the direction for us. 

AI prototyping beyond static screens

AI has also made prototyping much more powerful. We can move beyond static screens and create interactive ideas much earlier in the process.

Replit is our go-to for quick prototypes and web or product ideation, including live versions. Variant is another tool we use for fast web and product ideation, and it tends to push us in more creative directions. An interactive prototype in front of a client early on changes the conversation from “imagine this” to “try this.”

In fact, we did the design and frontend development for our client, Videobase (a video creator monetization platform), all within Replit.

We still used Figma for collaboration and feedback, but the actual live prototype helped the client visualize things that a flat Figma file wouldn’t: load effect, hover states, icon animations, graphs, etc.

What originality means for an AI-powered design studio

For us, originality is not about manually creating every single pixel. It’s about the idea, the art direction, the decisions, the combinations, and the final point of view. 

Originality is in the direction and decisions, not just who touched every pixel.

Because of that, we see the graphic designer becoming more of a creative director, editor, and curator, in addition to being a maker. That’s an upskill, not a replacement. It means clients working with an AI-powered design studio get sharper direction and more considered choices, not just more output. 

Using AI responsibly with client work

We love using AI to help brainstorm and speed up our design work, but we’re always super careful with it. We know how important client confidentiality and NDAs are, so we make sure to keep a close eye on exactly what information goes into any third-party AI tools.

Since AI data privacy can be a bit of a grey area and many tools learn from the data people type into them, we always keep our guard up.

When we’re working with high-profile clients or sensitive project details, we make a point to keep our prompts friendly but vague. We avoid using real brand names or specific client details in the tools so that your information stays completely safe, private, and just between us.

How to hire a design agency that uses AI strategically

The tools will keep changing, and the options they produce will keep multiplying. What separates original work from generic work is the same as it has always been: a clear direction and the judgment to know what’s worth keeping. 

If you’re wondering how to hire an ai designer, look for one that uses AI to sharpen its process, not replace its point of view.

We use AI to accelerate the process, not outsource the thinking.

entry.title: The 6 Reasons 79% of Our Design Clients Come Back
entry.summary: Dribbble Community Leader and Dtail Studio Founder Stan Hristov shares what keeps a design client for a decade: listening before you have an opinion, settling the money before you start, doing work nobody asked for, and why hardly any of it is about the design.
entry.content:
Dribbble Community Leader and Dtail Studio Founder Stan Hristov shares what keeps a design client for a decade: listening before you have an opinion, settling the money before you start, doing work nobody asked for, and why hardly any of it is about the design.

About the Author:
Stan Hristov leads Dtail Studio, a Barcelona-based branding and product design studio working with healthcare, AI and enterprise teams including Elli Cares, OXOS, Cinelytic, Evolus, Cubee, and more.

Of the clients we’ve worked with since 2019, 79% have come back with a second project. Some are on their fifth. A few have been with us for ten years, long enough that we’ve started redesigning things we designed the first time around.

Every time we look at why, the answer is almost never “the design was good.”

Good design is the entry fee. Every design studio a client is talking to can show them a beautiful screen, and the screen is almost never what the decision actually comes down to. What keeps people is everything around the work: how you handle a disagreement, how you spend their money, how often you interrupt them, and whether the invoice is ever a topic in the room.

Here’s the client retention strategy we’ve built.

1. We listen before having an opinion.

Fifteen years of building products doesn’t mean we know every business. It means we know how to find out quickly, and how to spot the moment something stops adding up.

The projects that reach us usually started as an idea someone carried around for months, sometimes years. They have already asked the whys and the hows. In the shower, at 2am, in a slightly tense conversation with a co-founder. They know things about their market that we are not going to learn from one discovery call and a competitor audit.

So the first stretch of any project is listening. Then asking. Then asking again.

Once we do understand the business, and not just the brief, we sometimes land somewhere different from the client. That is the moment we say so.

We bring a recommendation with the reasoning attached. Here’s what we’d do. Here’s why. Here’s what we think happens if we go the other way.

It’s still your company and your call, and plenty of times you’ll overrule us. Some of our best work came out of a client pushing back hard on something we were certain about. But nobody hires a studio for a pair of hands that agrees with them. You’re paying for the pattern recognition those years bought, and for our willingness to spend it in the room instead of saving it for the retrospective.

2. We commit to a direction early to protect the budget.

A wrong turn in week two costs a conversation. The same wrong turn in week nine costs a rebuild, and the client pays for it twice.

Our process is front-loaded on purpose. Strategic planning, then fast and wide exploration, then an actual decision before anything moves forward. Not “let’s keep both directions alive and see how everyone feels next week.” A decision, with a date on it.

That’s a budget argument at least as much as a creative one, and one of the simplest ways of avoiding scope creep in design projects.

Very little gets thrown away this way. That isn’t discipline for its own sake. It’s the client’s money staying inside the work instead of quietly leaking into rework nobody planned for.

3. We don’t bill for every Slack message.

The moment a client wonders whether a question is billable is the moment they stop asking. Clients who stop asking end up making decisions with less information than they had available.

Prescheduled weekly meetings. They’re short, they have something in them to decide, and they are not five people taking turns reading out what’s already in the file.

Everything in between happens in Slack. It’s one of our client communication best practices that costs us nothing and saves clients the most time. A quick answer, a second opinion, a sanity check on something that isn’t even ours. These are the small things that otherwise sit in a queue for six days and quietly stall a sprint, and we don’t put a meter on them.

Momentum is a deliverable. Most projects don’t die of bad work. They stall, very politely, while everyone waits for a calendar slot.

4. We settle payment upfront, every time.

Maybe you’re asking, “should design agencies charge upfront?” Taking payment in advance has nothing to do with cashflow nerves and everything to do with what an open invoice does to a project.

While money is unresolved, everything bends slightly around it. Studios start guarding scope. Clients start holding leverage. Somebody is mentally drafting a chase email during a design review. None of it gets said out loud and all of it lands in the work.

Settle it at the start and it disappears. Every conversation for the next three months is about the product, which is the only thing either side wanted to talk about in the first place. It also means both of us have committed to something real, so the relationship opens as two teams with one problem rather than a buyer keeping a vendor honest.

5. We do unbillable work that wasn’t asked for.

It’s terrible business advice, which is exactly why it works. Nobody makes a free thing for a client they don’t care about, and clients can tell the difference immediately.

Designers here draw for fun. There’s no policy and no slide about innovation time. It’s simply what people who like this job do on a Thursday evening, and more often than not the thing they’re pushing belongs to a client’s project, because that’s what has been living in their head all week. A different take on an onboarding flow. An illustration direction nobody asked for. A logo lockup that fixes something we’d all quietly noticed and nobody had raised.

When something good comes out of it, we send it over. No change order, no note about how this would fall outside the current scope. Sometimes it gets a polite no. Fairly often it becomes a thing.

“Half the things we ended up loving most were never in the scope. They just turned up one morning with a note saying we thought you might like this.” – M. Campos, CTO, XRay Analytics

6. We choose projects we’re excited about.

What we’re looking for is a business the team actually wants to think about. 

Very often that’s early-stage: founders who turn up with far more conviction than budget, building something with a real chance of becoming special. Those are the projects our designers quietly compete to get on, and who wants to be on a project shapes the outcome more than anything written in the brief.

It’s also where design earns the most. The decisions a company makes in its first year are the ones it has to live inside for the next ten, and getting them right early is worth considerably more than correcting them later with a bigger budget and a worse mood.

We’re much less interested in work nobody in the studio is excited about, whatever number is attached to it. Everyone who has ever hired an agency knows exactly what that looks like when it arrives.

How our long-term design partnerships do the heavy lifting.

  1. The explaining stops. 

Nobody has to explain again why the brand sounds the way it does, or reopen a decision that was settled two years ago. Between us we remember not only what was chosen but what was rejected and why, which is the part that tends to disappear when a company switches agency and quietly ends up somewhere it has already been.

  1. Feedback gets faster and more honest. 

When there’s trust in the room, nobody softens a note into three sentences of diplomacy, and nobody reads a blunt one as an insult. A plain “no, this isn’t it” on a Tuesday can save two weeks.

  1. The direction holds, too. 

Instead of a pile of projects that each look like the year they were made in, the work starts to accumulate. Website, product, deck, campaign, all pulling the same way, because the same people have been carrying the reasoning the whole time.

  1. And then there’s freedom, which is the part designers care about most.

A client who has watched us be right, watched us be wrong, and seen how we handled both will greenlight the braver option. That isn’t a reward for loyalty. It’s simply what becomes possible once nobody is auditioning any more.

Is your designer the right one for the long-haul?

If you’re compiling questions to ask before hiring a product designer, don’t just check what their last project looked like. Ask what happened the first time they disagreed with a client. Ask what happened when something went wrong. Ask whether anyone from the original team is still on the account.

The answers to those tell you far more about the next twelve months than any portfolio will.

entry.title: The Box Design System: AI-Ready Figma Files for Enterprise Software
entry.summary: Dribbble Community Leaders and Flexy Global co-founders Avetisyan, Gabrielyan, and Saroka reveal their Box Design System for structuring complex Figma files, helping both developers and AI coding agents understand product behavior without the guesswork.
entry.content:
Dribbble Community Leaders and Flexy Global co-founders Avetisyan, Gabrielyan, and Saroka reveal their Box Design System for structuring complex Figma files, helping both developers and AI coding agents understand product behavior without the guesswork.

About the Authors:
Garik Avetisyan, Davit Gabrielyan, and Anastasia Saroka are co-founders of Flexy Global, a design and development partner for startups and global enterprises. Garik built and successfully exited a consumer app used by millions. Davit brings 15 years of experience leading complex projects and operations at international companies including Orange (France Telecom) and Coca-Cola Hellenic. Anastasia, Design Director at Flexy Global, brings experience designing products for large corporations and startups in the fitness industry. Together, they explore how better design systems and development practices can help teams build complex technology more clearly and efficiently.

On a recent enterprise software project, we were working with a Figma file that needed to support both traditional developer handoff and AI-assisted development. One section alone contained dozens of screens documenting a single part of the product.

Each screen made sense on its own. The difficulty was understanding how they belonged together.

For the designers and developers who had worked on the project for months, much of that context was already familiar. We knew which screens represented the starting point, what action caused each change, which states were alternatives, and which details were still under discussion.

A coding agent coming to the file had none of that background. An individual screen did not provide enough context to explain the complete behavior, while the full canvas introduced too much unrelated information. We needed a way to organize the relevant frames, states, and decisions around a single interaction so they could be understood and used more effectively in AI-assisted development. That need became the basis of our Box Design System.

What is the Box Design System?

The Box Design System is our method for organizing complex product behavior into bounded sections of the Figma canvas. Each box contains the screens, states, transitions, annotations, and implementation context needed to understand one part of the product. This makes the file easier for people to navigate while also preparing its structure for AI-assisted development.

In the enterprise platform we were designing, navigation alone included several connected behaviors. Users could interact with a floating bar, select assets, explore the map directly, or move through a hierarchy. All of these actions occurred within the same broader interface, but they did not belong to the same flows.

Placing every screen in one large sequence would have made the file look complete while leaving its logic ambiguous. Instead, we grouped related states into separate boxes such as “Floating Bar,” “Select Assets,” “Direct Map Exploration,” and “Hierarchy.” Each box represented one coherent part of the experience.

At first, this was a way to make a complicated canvas easier for people to navigate. As AI agents became part of the development workflow, the boxes gained another purpose: they created clearer units of context for implementation.

Here are four principles that shaped the system.

1. Organize boxes around behavior, not pages

A page is a visual container. It is not always a useful development boundary.

One page may contain several independent interactions. A single interaction may also extend across panels, overlays, menus, and several screen states.

In our project, selecting an asset and exploring the map took place within the same primary interface. Visually, the screens shared most of their structure. Functionally, however, they represented different behaviors.

Treating them as one group would require a developer or agent to determine which changes belonged to asset selection and which belonged to map exploration. That distinction was obvious to the team because we had discussed it repeatedly. It was not necessarily visible in the pixels.

We therefore organized the boxes as a hierarchy rather than treating every box as an equal unit. The system has three levels:

  • Feature boxes represent a complete product capability, such as Navigation.
  • Flow boxes sit inside the feature box and separate interactions such as “Select Assets” and “Direct Map Exploration.”
  • Screen-state boxes sit inside each flow and name the specific action or state shown on every screen.

This structure allows someone to move from the broader feature to an individual flow and then to the exact screen behavior without losing the relationship between them. It also means that an implementation task can be scoped around the behavior the team needs to build, rather than every element visible on the page.

2. Make each box understandable on its own

A useful box should not require a guided tour from the designer who created it.

Someone opening the file should be able to understand what the interaction does, where it begins, and what changes as the user moves through it.

That does not mean duplicating every piece of product documentation inside Figma. It means including enough context to remove the most consequential ambiguity.

Depending on the feature, a box may contain:

  • The default or entry state
  • The action available to the user
  • The resulting state
  • Expanded and collapsed variations
  • Selected, disabled, empty, loading, or error states
  • Short notes explaining behavior that cannot be understood visually
  • References to existing components or patterns

This self-contained structure matters for human teams, especially when people join a project late or return to a feature after several weeks. It matters even more for coding agents.

An agent does not have the memory of the workshop where the interaction was discussed. It does not know which Slack message changed the requirement or which visual difference was intentional. It can only work with the context it is given.

If critical information sits somewhere else on the canvas, remains buried in a comment thread, or exists only in the team’s memory, the agent must infer what is missing.

And inference is where avoidable mistakes begin.

3. Make interactions and transitions visible

Individual screens show different interface states, but they do not always explain how the user moves between them.

In our design files, we use simple arrows to connect an interaction with the screen or state it produces. If clicking a button opens a sidebar, we connect that action to the designed sidebar state. If an interaction takes the user to another screen, the arrow shows exactly where they will arrive.

Not every interaction needs this treatment. Adding arrows to simple or obvious actions can create unnecessary visual noise. They become particularly useful when one screen contains several possible interactions, each leading to a different state or part of the flow.

For someone who has worked on the product for months, these relationships may already feel obvious. Developers and AI agents do not necessarily have that context. Without a visible connection, an agent may recognize all the individual screens but still misunderstand which action produces which result.

Combined with the box hierarchy, these connections make both the structure and sequence of the experience easier to follow. The boxes show which screens belong to the same feature and flow, while the arrows explain how users move between them. It is a simple practice, but it reduces how much developers and agents need to infer from the designs.

4. Give the AI agent a bounded unit of context

AI coding tools can now access much more than a screenshot. When connected through tools such as the Figma MCP server, an agent can retrieve structured design information, visual references, variables, components, and layout data from a selected part of a file. However, in AI-assisted development, access to more information does not automatically lead to a better understanding of what needs to be built.

An isolated frame may leave out the surrounding states required to understand a behavior. At the other extreme, a large page or full canvas may introduce unrelated screens, unresolved concepts, and several versions of the same feature. The Box Design System creates a practical middle layer between these two extremes.

Instead of asking an agent to “build this page,” a developer can direct it toward a bounded interaction containing the relevant states, transitions, and supporting context. This gives the agent enough information to understand the intended behavior without requiring it to interpret the entire product.

The boundary of a box does not need to match a single code component. Some boxes may translate into one component, while others may involve several components and application states. The box is there to define the product behavior being implemented, not to dictate the final code architecture.

The quality of the generated code still depends on the codebase, prompts, design-system implementation, and the agent’s access to existing components. Figma also recommends semantic naming, variables, Auto Layout, reusable components, annotations, and Code Connect to improve consistency. The boxes complement this infrastructure by organizing those elements into a coherent piece of product behavior that the agent can understand and act on.

What boxes cannot solve

A clean Figma canvas cannot compensate for an undefined product.

If the team has not decided how an interaction should behave, placing its screens inside a box will not resolve the underlying uncertainty. It may simply make that uncertainty easier to see.

That is still valuable.

When related states are placed together, inconsistencies become more visible. The team may discover two competing versions of the same behavior, an exception with no recovery path, or a state that was discussed but never designed.

Boxes also do not replace the platform’s design system. While the main design file uses boxes to organize screens, flows, and product behavior, the design system lives in a separate Figma file containing the shared components, variants, and variables used across those designs.

The design system does not need to follow a box-design hierarchy, but it should be structured and detailed enough for agents to understand exactly what they need and where to find it in the file. Clear naming, logical grouping, and consistent component structures help both developers and AI agents find and reuse the correct elements. Without that structure and the corresponding code, an agent may understand the intended behavior while still selecting the wrong component or creating unnecessary one-off elements.

The box defines the scope and behavior. The design system defines how the interface should be constructed. The codebase defines how it must function in production.

Why Figma file structure now matters for AI-assisted development

For years, design-file organization was often treated as an internal concern. A tidy file was easier to navigate, easier to hand off, and kinder to the next designer who had to work in it.

That is no longer the full story.

As design files become direct inputs to AI-assisted development, their structure begins to influence what an agent understands, what it overlooks, and how much it must infer.

The canvas is no longer only a place where the team presents the final interface. It is becoming part of the system through which software gets built.

Our box-based approach began with a practical need: make a complicated enterprise product easier to understand. Its value grew when the same structure helped divide that product into clearer units for implementation and review.

The boxes themselves are not the innovation. The clarity they create is.

Components define what the interface is made from. Frames capture individual moments. Boxes explain how those moments belong together and what the team is trying to build.

In a development process increasingly shared with AI agents, that context is no longer optional documentation.

It is part of the product.
