entry.title: How To Launch a Brand in 90 Days: A Proven System for Shelf-Ready CPG
entry.summary: Dribbble Community Leader and MAVRK Studio Founder & CEO Aaron Swinton breaks down the agency's integrated 90-day launch strategy that reshaped clients' go-to-market approach and generated results.
entry.content:
Dribbble Community Leader and MAVRK Studio Founder & CEO Aaron Swinton breaks down the agency's integrated 90-day launch strategy that reshaped clients' go-to-market approach and generated results.

About the Author:
Aaron Swinton is the Founder and CEO of MAVRK Studio, where he handles business strategy, client partnerships, and the agency’s growth. He has experience in brand building, venture investing, fundraising, and operations, and he uses it to help CPG brands launch and grow.

Most consumer packaged goods (CPG) launches don’t last. Somewhere between 70% and 85% fail, and it’s rarely because the product was bad. 

More often, the launch itself is the problem. There’s a logo from one shop, packaging from another, a website from a third, and nobody owning the whole picture. Along the way, teams end up testing the new product instead of the consumer need, the category, or the retail plan. 

An integrated CPG launch strategy fixes that by lining up product, brand, packaging, eCommerce, and marketing in one plan. That’s the idea behind MAVRK’s 90-day launch system, where Day 90 means “shelf-ready and launch-ready.” 

Why Most CPG Launches Fail (and How a 90-Day Plan Fixes It)

  • Fragmented vendors: Brand, packaging, and digital are split across separate teams, and nobody owns the whole launch.
    The Fix: One team building all three in parallel.
  • Unvalidated positioning: Design starts before anyone has confirmed demand, price, or the competition.
    The Fix: Validate all three before design begins.
  • Weak execution: Wrong labels, bad dimensions, and missed retailer requirements derail a good product.
    The Fix: A week-by-week calendar with owners, approvals, and checkpoints.

One honest note: 90 days is the target, and it assumes timely feedback. Plan a few extra days for each round of revisions.

Inside the 90-Day CPG Launch Plan

Our plan runs on six overlapping workstreams instead of one long list of tasks. Across them, the work moves through four phases: foundation, build, pre-launch, and launch. 

  • Weeks 1–2, Validate & Position: the product and launch strategy
  • Weeks 2–4, Build the Brand: identity and messaging system
  • Weeks 3–7, Design for the Shelf: compliant, retail-ready packaging
  • Weeks 5–10, Build the Launch Engine: website, eCommerce, email capture
  • Weeks 7–11, Create the Content: photo, video, social, launch creative
  • Weeks 9–12, Get Shelf & Launch Ready: sales materials and retail readiness 

It all lives in a week-by-week calendar with clear owners, approvals, and go/no-go checkpoints. Because the workstreams overlap, packaging and photography can share one creative brief, and creator outreach can start before creative is finished. 

Weeks 1–2: Validate and Position

Prove Demand Before You Launch a CPG Brand

Design is the fun part, so it’s tempting to start there. But a CPG product needs category validation first: is the need real, where does the price sit, and who are you up against? 

The right research depends on how much the brand has already decided. For a brand with a clear product and launch direction, we review the category, competitors, and audience to sharpen its positioning before design begins. If the opportunity itself is still open, a deeper Opportunity Sprint can come first.

Depending on the scope, that work may include:

  • A shelf and competitor review to understand the category and identify gaps
  • Customer research and interviews to test assumptions and hear how people describe the need
  • An assessment of the audience, differentiation, and best channels for launch

The goal is to make the key decisions early, so the brand, packaging, website, and launch content can move forward with a shared direction.

For instance, take our work for REALI. We redid branding, packaging, web design, social media and directed their go to market into colleges & gyms vs traditional retail. They’ve since gotten into 30+ stores in 5 months.

From Consumer Language to a Clear Promise

Research only helps if it turns into a promise people understand. Your positioning is that bridge, and it shapes everything after it. 

A positioning section of your launch plan should include:

  • Frame of reference (the category you’re competing in)
  • Target consumer
  • Key benefit
  • Reason to believe
  • A promise and brand story in real consumer language
  • A one-line concept statement everyone can defend 

These decisions ripple into recipe choices, pack size, pricing, channels, and the retail pitch. 

Weeks 2–4: Build the Brand

Positioning tells you who the brand is for. Now it needs a look and a voice people recognize. 

  • Naming exploration, checked for trademark, domain, and social handles early, ideally in week 2 
  • Logo, color palette, typography, and core visual language
  • A brand voice brief: three personality words, plus “we are / we are not”
  • A documented brand system: promise, personality, voice, messaging pillars, visual direction 
  • A brand guidelines doc, even a single page, so every vendor works from the same reference 

Weeks 3–7: Design for the Shelf

Packaging, Compliance, and Operations

Plenty of launches stumble at the execution layer: wrong labels, bad dimensions, missed routing guides, or claims that don’t comply. 

This phase turns your positioning into a full SKU architecture, label system, and production files. 

Your packaging and operations checklist:

  • Front-of-pack hierarchy, with a clear benefit
  • Nutrition and regulatory compliance
  • GTIN/UPC and case pack structure
  • Co-packer alignment, lead times, and freight
  • Retailer documentation confirmed before launch 

A quick shelf test: does it stand out at thumbnail size, and would a creator want to hold it? 

Retail-ready doesn’t mean retail-first. Build a few months of online sales (or community) proof before pitching buyers. 

Weeks 5–10: Build the Launch Engine

Website, eCommerce, and Email

Even retail-first brands need a strong digital engine for education, storytelling, lead capture, and proof for buyers. In Weeks 5–10, we build a conversion-focused website, eCommerce setup, store locator, and email flows.

  • The Rice Cream: branding, packaging, web design, and launch content built to tell the product story and drive early interest.
  • REALI: eCommerce-ready web design and launch messaging aligned with packaging and photo/video. 

What your plan should include:

  • Landing pages and lead magnets
  • A pre-launch waitlist
  • Abandoned-cart flows and post-purchase emails 
  • A pre-launch email list goal of 500+ subscribers 

Weeks 7–11: Create the Content

Photo, Video, and Social

Content turns a launch plan from strategy into visible momentum across social, email, and paid channels. In Weeks 7–11, we produce product photography, lifestyle imagery, recipe or usage content, and launch videos. 

Folkland’s social launch campaign shows what consistent visuals and storytelling can do. 

The Rice Cream and REALI paired photo, video, and social content that matched their packaging and websites. 

Map content to each phase:

  • Pre-launch: teasers, behind-the-scenes, a countdown series 
  • Launch: reveal content, how-to clips, UGC prompts, retailer-specific creatives 
  • Post-launch: put more behind what worked, and feed real customer content and reviews back in

Creators can support each phase of the launch, from early product introductions to launch-day content and customer reviews. Depending on the brand, we may build a broader affiliate program where creators earn a commission on sales, or work with a smaller group of carefully chosen influencers to reach a specific audience.

Weeks 9–12: Get Shelf & Launch Ready

Go-to-Market Execution: Launch Week to Post-Launch

Build your launch calendar across pre-launch, launch, and post-launch, with inventory, media, and in-store support all lined up. 

In launch week, point every channel at one clear call to action, concentrate spend in the first 2–4 weeks, and check velocity and feedback daily. 

We treat the first 90 days in market as a commercial test, with success metrics and go/no-go or pivot points built into the plan. 

Track:

  • Velocity: how fast the product sells
  • Repeat rate
  • ROAS: return on ad spend
  • Email opt-ins 

When a message or creative performs well, we put more budget behind it and use what we learn to brief the next round of creators. When results are weak, we review the data, adjust the approach, and shift spend toward what’s working.

Alongside the launch, the sales side gets ready with a retail pitch built on your online sales data, plus sales materials and retailer documentation.

Growing After Launch: Community and Revenue

A strong launch strategy connects to a growth plan. It doesn’t stop at Day 90. MAVRK Grow picks up where launch leaves off. 

  • Community growth: organic social, content, email, creator activation, and IRL activations. 
  • Revenue growth: paid media, performance creative, and conversion optimization to scale what worked. 

Early signals, like top creatives, strongest audiences, and best regions, feed straight into performance campaigns. 

Putting It All Together: A 90-Day Checklist

  • Days 1–30: validate, position, name, and build your brand identity and guidelines
  • Days 31–60: packaging, online store, photography, creator outreach
  • Days 61–90: content, email list, ad setup, soft launch, creator launch day, public launch 

The steps that prevent failure: validation, coherent branding, retail-ready packaging, a digital launch engine, and aligned marketing. We swap a pile of vendors for one accountable team. 

Your next step: audit your current launch plan against this checklist, or sketch your own 90-day roadmap before you talk to designers, agencies, or co-packers.

You can also talk to us about your brand’s starting point and launch goals, and we’ll help you work out what your first 90 days should look like.

entry.title: B2B Brand Strategy: How To Transition from Founder Equity to Company Equity
entry.summary: Dribbble Community Leader and Brandly Founder Zlatina Petrova discusses how founders can turn executive trust into lasting company equity.
entry.content:
Dribbble Community Leader and Brandly Founder Zlatina Petrova discusses how founders can turn executive trust into lasting company equity.

About the Author:

Zlatina Petrova has spent 13 years shaping brands and digital products across Silicon Valley and Europe. As Founder and Design Director of Brandly, she works with tech startups, VCs, global brands and government institutions including work on Bulgaria’s national design system. Her work sits between branding, product design and UX/UI, with a belief that design should do more than look good: it should help businesses grow, products work better and brands mean something to people.

When Brandly started, clients weren’t buying the company. They were buying the people behind it. I already had a solid reputation of my own: I had led product design at an LA-based startup, worked as a creative director in Florida, and won one of Europe’s most prestigious design awards.

The media were dying to interview me. Nobody was dying to interview Brandly. Same with the clients. They trusted me first, and the company second. Trust lived in the founder before it lived in the brand. This is the core of effective executive personal branding. Only later did Brandly accumulate enough history, language, and systems to carry that trust independently.

In that transition, one truth became obvious: people don’t experience companies first. They experience people.

In the early stages, a founder’s personal brand is not a vanity project sitting next to the company brand. In a founder-led business, it is often the first interface through which people decide whether your company deserves attention at all.

Before they understand your product or mission statement, they are asking much simpler questions:

  • Do I trust this person?
  • Do I believe what they believe?
  • Do I want to listen to them?
  • Do I want to work with them?

The personal brand becomes so closely attached to the company that the founder eventually becomes the bottleneck for trust. If they step away, clients become nervous. If they move on to something new, the company suddenly feels different. If they want to sell the business, part of its value is still sitting inside one person’s relationships, reputation and way of thinking.

The founder’s real job goes far beyond visibility. The job is to turn personal conviction into something the company can eventually carry without you. Here is how the founder shapes the brand around them, and how that personal equity eventually becomes company equity.

Establishing Brand Identity and The Founder’s Role In Corporate Branding

Inevitable brands rarely begin as systems. They begin as conviction. Before there are guidelines, culture decks, and campaigns, there is usually one person who sees something that does not yet fully exist.

That person has to believe in it long enough for everybody else to catch up.

This is what I mean by devotion. Not founder mythology, and definitely not “hustle culture.” I mean feeling the brand deeply enough to sense when something strengthens it and when something quietly weakens it.

In the beginning, you notice the wrong tone in a sentence, the product that makes money but weakens positioning, or the impressive partnership that simply does not belong in the world you are building. Over time, your instinct teaches the rest of the organization what the brand actually is.

When the founder cares deeply about the details, employees start making better decisions without constant approval. What started as one person’s conviction slowly becomes something shared.

If the founder carries the brand internally, the personal brand makes that worldview visible externally. But this is where many founders get personal branding wrong.

Your personal brand is not a diary of everything you think, eat, or do. It is the clearest public expression of the parts of you that give the company meaning: your judgment, beliefs, standards, taste, expertise and way of seeing the world.

The public version of you should still be true. Just edited. You do not need to publish every private detail to feel human; you just need to make the part of you that explains the company legible to others.

Takeaway: The founder shapes the brand from the inside first. Personal branding makes that worldview visible from the outside.

Core Value Alignment and Strategic Brand Development for B2B Founders

There is a strange ritual happening in branding workshops everywhere, including plenty of B2B brand strategy consulting sessions we’ve run ourselves. Someone opens a Miro board. Everyone gets virtual sticky notes. Forty-five minutes later, almost every company on Earth discovers its values are innovation, integrity, excellence and customer-centricity.

If your competitors can copy your values without changing a word, they are not your values.

Real values are inconvenient. They come from your experience: the managers you never wanted to become, the moments that made you proud, the clients you instinctively protect, and the compromises you refuse even when money is on the table.

This is where founder branding begins. Not with “What should I post about?” but with “What do I believe so strongly that it repeatedly changes my decisions?”

Founders encode their values into the company whether they intend to or not. Those values dictate:

  • Who gets hired
  • How fast the product ships
  • Whether difficult conversations are had
  • What the company quietly tolerates

Repeated decisions become culture. Culture becomes user experience. Experience becomes reputation. Reputation becomes a brand.

Try building a founder value map. Take five important moments from your professional life, especially the frustrations and failures. Ask: What did this teach me that I now believe very strongly?

Look for repetition. You may discover that five apparently unrelated stories express the same principle. “Care” is not a value until it changes how you price projects or communicate bad news. A brand becomes credible when values create visible trade-offs.

Takeaway: Your founder brand should be built from beliefs with consequences, not values that simply look good on a wall.

Thought Leadership Strategy and Elevating Your Executive Personal Brand

Founders often tell me they “should be posting more.” I’m not convinced.

The internet does not urgently need another founder sharing seven lessons from waking up at 5 AM. What people need from experts is not more content. They need judgment.

A strong founder brand gives people a sense of how you think, what you challenge, and what matters to you before they ever buy.

A brand identity designer can post: “Five branding trends for 2026.” Or they can say: “Most early-stage companies redesign their visual identity too early, because the real problem is they haven’t decided what they want to be remembered for.”

The first gives me information. The second gives me perspective. Perspective is invaluable in businesses where clients buy trust: consulting, law, venture, architecture, or complex B2B software. A case study tells me what you did; a point of view tells me how you’ll think when we hit a problem neither of us has seen before.

A true thought leadership strategy begins with three questions:

  • What do I believe?
  • What observation made me believe it?
  • What do I do differently because of it?

A belief that never changes your behavior is just positioning copy. For example, we believe brand consistency shouldn’t depend on designers policing assets. So, what do we do differently? We treat governance and contribution rules as part of the design itself, not an afterthought.

Now, you aren’t just claiming expertise; you are showing how it changes your work.

Takeaway: Don’t use your personal brand to prove that you are visible. Use it to make your thinking visible. 

Brand Cultivation and Hiring for Corporate Brand Alignment

Who is helping you build this thing?

Customers experience your brand through a salesperson, support agent, designer, freelancer, and sometimes a vendor. Every one of them translates the brand through hundreds of micro-decisions. A brilliant person who repeatedly makes choices that feel wrong for the company can weaken the brand more than an average logo ever will.

The best teams develop a shared instinct. They know which compromise the company will make and which it won’t. They know when something is technically correct but still not right.

You can call this cultural fit or brand alignment. The outcome is what matters: the person amplifies the signal rather than introducing static.

This must influence hiring. Assess skill, but also ask questions that reveal taste and judgment:

  • Show candidates real scenarios.
  • Ask what they would protect when time runs out.
  • Ask what they refuse to compromise on.

Look at your existing team with the same honesty. Who strengthens the brand? Who is excellent at their job but consistently pulls the company toward a different identity? Alignment cannot be ignored forever.

Takeaway: Skills determine whether someone can do the job. Alignment determines whether they strengthen the brand while doing it.

Enterprise Brand Architecture: Scaling from Founder to Corporate Entity

As the brand grows, the founder’s role changes. Early on, trust travels through the person. Clients use your reputation as a shortcut to decide if the business is credible. But growth demands a new question: where should that trust travel next?

This brand equity transfer is crucial. Brand architecture dictates how much of the founder’s reputation transfers to the company, how much remains with the founder, and which new offers borrow from either.

Founders are tempted to capitalize on momentum. If people trust you, it’s tempting to endorse every new service or product you launch. Sometimes that is smart. Sometimes it is simply logo slapping. Accumulated trust should only travel where the promise and experience justify it.

Navigating this is why companies hire a specialized brand architecture agency, but you can start with three core paths:

  • The Unified Brand: If a new offer delivers the same core promise and experience, it belongs inside a unified brand. The goal is to move trust away from the founder and deeper into the company.
  • The Endorsed Brand (Brand Extension): If the experience belongs to the same world but the promise is different, it’s a brand extension. A visible association (“From the founder of…”) reduces perceived risk without pretending the new venture is just another version of the parent company.
  • The Individual Brand: If the new offer has a completely different promise and audience, forcing the founder’s name onto it creates confusion. Founder equity shouldn’t be permission to attach the same reputation to everything.

The strategic goal is to make the founder an endorsement layer, not a permanent dependency.

Early on, use your personal brand. Let your name open doors and reduce risk. But simultaneously, the company must accumulate its own evidence: recognizable methodologies, systems, and a consistent experience.

The founder says, “This is what I believe.” The company proves, “This is how we operate.” Eventually, the customer concludes, “I trust this organization, even when the founder is not in the room.”

Many founder-led companies fail to reach this point, and Brandly was no exception early on. If the founder remains the ultimate source of reassurance, it becomes a massive problem the moment they want to step back, launch something new, or sell.

The best transition is gradual:

  • Give visibility to your team.
  • Turn personal know-how into company methodology.
  • Move recurring ideas from your LinkedIn posts into the company’s language.
  • Let clients form relationships beyond you.

Make the experience consistent enough that your personal reputation becomes the introduction, not the entire argument.

In maturity, the founder brand and company brand stop competing for attention and start endorsing each other.

Takeaway: In the beginning, the founder lends trust to the company. During growth, convert that borrowed trust into company equity. Use brand architecture to decide where that trust should compound, endorse, or stop.

People may buy the founder before they buy the company. That is not a weakness to hide; it is an advantage to design deliberately. But the founder’s real job is to build a world compelling enough that, eventually, people no longer need them standing at the entrance.

entry.title: Healthcare Tech Design: Rebranding Kinetik’s NEMT Platform
entry.summary: Dribbble Community Leader and Afternow Brand & Web Lead Vicente Reyes Montealegre shares Kinetik's NEMT platform rebrand, balancing warmth and trust for coordinators and patients with opposite needs.
entry.content:
Dribbble Community Leader and Afternow Brand & Web Lead Vicente Reyes Montealegre shares Kinetik's NEMT platform rebrand, balancing warmth and trust for coordinators and patients with opposite needs.

About the Author:
Vicente Reyes Montealegre, heads Afternow’s Brand and Web teams to guide SaaS companies, enterprises, and fast-growing startups in their digital journeys. The agency’s work spans strategy, brand, website, product and development, all under one roof, all connected to one vision.

Access to care was the whole point of Kinetik’s business. Non-emergency medical transport gets patients to dialysis, to chemo, to appointments they’d otherwise skip. So, the actual brief for this patient coordination platform design ran much deeper than logos and layouts. We needed to build a comprehensive product people could trust their care to.

The American healthcare system doesn’t make that simple. Riders, providers, and insurers all operate on different timelines and different systems, and getting them to coordinate can be exhausting for everyone involved, patients included. Kinetik exists to make that coordination actually work.

That’s a different problem than what most HealthTech faces. Kinetik’s users weren’t optimizing a workflow. Many were older, managing a condition, coordinating a ride they couldn’t afford to miss. Every decision, on the brand, the site, the products, had to hold up under that weight.

Warmth as a design compass in healthcare branding

We moved away from the clinical, high-tech blue and aqua gradients the old identity relied on. Most health tech platforms reach for a look that leans too much on the tech and not so much on what health means. It’s a common pitfall you’ll notice when browsing portfolios of even highly rated brand identity designers.

It makes sense because that is where innovation sat ten years ago. Today, we can argue that audiences are craving for digital experiences that feel tangible, genuine, with more texture and life in them.

The inspiration point started with a very concrete moment of Kinetik’s users journey: the feeling of looking out a window on a ride, watching the city go by as they travel to their medical appointments. That image is where the painterly, almost impressionistic illustrations of the urban landscape came from.

The palette followed the same instinct, pulled from the organic rather than the artificial: deep and vivid greens against gold, salmon, lavender, and a purple that reads like the last light of a sunset. Nothing else in the category looks like this.

Typography carries a similar weight. An elegant serif, used large, gives the brand a voice instead of blending into the next healthcare login screen. Used small, it steps back and lets the content do the work.

The photography direction stays close to that same idea, people in ordinary moments, at home, in the city, living their lives. Access to care isn’t confined to a hospital visit, it shows up in every part of someone’s day.

The refreshed logo carries this story as well. A capital K, drawn in one curved stroke, with a dot sitting at the end like a destination marker, because getting somewhere is what Kinetik actually does.

Structuring medical website navigation for complex audiences

The marketing site had one real problem before the rebrand: articles, case studies, and news all sat in one undifferentiated pile. We split it apart, and built the site’s structure and navigation around the three groups Kinetik actually serves: health plans, transportation providers, and state and government agencies, each with a clear path through the site instead of one menu trying to work for everyone.

The website does more than tell the story here. The same visual language that sets the mood on the landing page also gets used inside the product screen visualisations, to flag a trip, a claim waiting on review, or a step someone shouldn’t skip. Same system, pulling double duty: telling the story, and pointing at what matters.

HealthTech products solving opposite users at once

Inside the products, the same question got harder. Coordinators needed dense, fast interfaces, real-time visibility across thousands of trips, quick assignment, no wasted motion. Patients using the Kinetik Health app needed almost the reverse: large touch targets, few steps, a calm interface that doesn’t rush them.

That tension sits at the center of the patient app. Real-time tracking and recurring scheduling are genuinely sophisticated features. They had to live inside something simple enough for someone managing a visual or cognitive impairment to use without a second thought.

Contrast, focus states, type size, motion, none of it was a checklist item added at the end. It shaped the product from the start, proving exactly why companies must look beyond aesthetics when vetting UI/UX designers. Confusion on this screen costs someone their ride to treatment.

What it takes to build a healthcare product patients can rely on

The brand is the part people notice first, the color palette, the painterly illustrations, the typographic voice. It’s the part that makes Kinetik stand out on a shelf full of competitors that forgot about the people they’ll be affecting the most. That matters. But a harder, quieter work sits underneath: the architecture, the user flows, the structure that holds four different products together for four very different users. That work is the proof point, and the reason a patient with a ride booked for 7am can actually get there.
